title: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Visual Perception” (from p. 577), p. 581. Scope: human visual texture perception

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Behavioral and neural datasets support direct tests of local-feature models for selected textures. They do not cover perception generally, and rival hierarchical models can produce similar response patterns.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit models based on densities of local feature-detector responses to human texture-discrimination behavior and neural recordings, comparing them with models using higher-order spatial relations. Superior out-of-sample prediction by density-only models supports the account; systematic metamers or discriminations they miss refute its generality.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Local feature density is correlated with higher-order texture statistics.

Mouse neural data do not directly establish human perception.

The claim ranges beyond vision to perception generally.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.5
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Texture discrimination by local-feature statistics is a standard, operational hypothesis, and public texture sets plus cortical atlases contain the relevant variables. Those data support a density or summary-statistic account for many textures and also contain known counterexamples that need higher-order structure. The claim's extension to perception in general, by analogy with color, is wider than this test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Represent textures by densities of a fixed set of local templates and test whether those densities predict human discrimination as well as joint statistics or less structured image measures. Prediction from densities, with cortical responses matching the templates, would support the claim; systematic failures on textures that share densities but differ in dependencies would refute the density account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The broader claim that perception in general ignores everything but fixed features exceeds texture data.

Some texture pairs are discriminated by joint statistics even when marginal feature densities match.
